replies.text:
​@konstantinNass First of all, there is a difference between Turks and Turkic peoples. They sound similar, but they don't mean exactly the same thing. Turkish usually refers to the people and language of Turkiye, while Turkic is a broader term that includes different peoples and languages, such as Kazakh, Azerbaijani, Uzbek, Turkmen, and Kyrgyz.

Turkic identity and history did not begin with the Ottoman Empire. Turkic speaking peoples and their cultures existed centuries before the Ottoman Empire was established. The Göktürk Khaganate, for example, existed long before the Ottomans.

The Xiongnu also played an important role in the history of the Eurasian steppe, although their exact ethnic and linguistic origins are still debated.

Also Mongolians and Turkic peoples can be described as as cousins. They have lived alongside each other for centuries, shared cultural influences, interacted, traded, fought wars, and formed alliances. Some populations also share ancestry. However, they are two distinct groups with different language families and histories. Their exact ancient relationship is still debated.

And yes, history absolutely plays a role in biology. Historical migrations, population movements, and intermarriage help explain why populations share ancestry.

However, Turks did not originate from Greeks, and Greeks and Turks were not one single ethnic group. Their populations interacted, migrated, and intermarried throughout history, which naturally contributed to shared ancestry. This doesn't make Greeks Turkish or Turks Greek. Both populations have their own identities, cultures, languages, and histories.

My original point was simply that neighbouring populations can share ancestry without having the same ethnic identity. I believe we should respect people's identities instead of trying to claim ownership over each other's ancestors.
